title: Which four questions decide whether a client should enter a new market?
description: "Should the client enter this market?" A new country, customer segment or product category.
hook: Market entry is a classic case: should the client go into a new country, segment or product category? It helps to remember there are only four questions underneath it. Here they are, and how to use them.
body:
When you will use it

A new country, customer segment or product category.

This is a decide question: "Should we do this?" Test it against a few yes/no questions, put a number on it, and end with a clear yes or no. More on the three families of case questions.

Ask this first

Why this market, and what would success look like, by when?

The structure

  • Is the market attractive?
    • Size and growth
    • Typical margins
    • Barriers to entry
  • Can we win?
    • Competitors and their strength
    • What customers need
    • Our edge
  • Will it pay? (compare with payback target)
    • Revenue we can expect
    • Running costs
    • Upfront investment
  • Can we pull it off?
    • Capabilities we lack (decides build, partner or buy)
    • Timing and pilot
    • Key risks

Make it your own

The prize = market size × the share you can win × margin. Compare it with the upfront investment, then say how you would enter.

The mistake to avoid

Describing the market at length but never comparing the prize with the cost of getting in.

Practise with real prompts

1. Should a luxury hotel group launch a budget hotel brand?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Size and growth of budget hotels; Competitors and their returns
  • Economics: Cost to build or convert, room rates, occupancy; Return vs our cost of capital
  • Fit and risk: Can we run low-cost hotels well?; Damage to the luxury brand
  • Cannibalisation: Guests who would trade down from our hotels; Net new profit

Where to start: Economics per hotel: if a single hotel doesn't make money, nothing else matters.

The trap: Forgetting the brand risk and cannibalisation for an existing luxury group.

2. Should a coffee chain sell its beans in supermarkets?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Size of premium coffee in supermarkets; Competitors and shelf space
  • Economics: Price, retailer margin, our cost; Volume needed to pay back
  • Cannibalisation and halo: Café visits lost vs new customers; Brand awareness gained
  • Brand and operations: Premium image on a shelf next to discounts; Roasting and supply capacity

Where to start: Net profit after the café visits we might lose.

The trap: Ignoring the effect on café visits and on a premium brand.

3. Should an airline launch a daily London–Lagos route?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: Demand by segment: business, visiting family, cargo; Seasonality
  • Competition: Rivals' flights, prices, loyalty; Likely response
  • Economics: Revenue per flight vs cost per flight; Aircraft we would take from other routes
  • Risks: Currency, repatriating cash; Airport slots and approvals

Where to start: Profit per flight vs what the aircraft earns elsewhere.

The trap: Forgetting the opportunity cost of the aircraft.
